people.name: Mother Mary Alfred Moes
body: On August 21, 1883, a tornado tore through Rochester, Minnesota. It killed dozens of people and injured many more, and the town had no hospital. The injured were taken to makeshift sites, including the convent of the Sisters of St. Francis. The sisters, most of them trained as teachers rather than nurses, cared for the wounded alongside Dr. William Worrall Mayo.

Moes was born Maria Catherine Moes in Remich, Luxembourg, a small, mostly Catholic country. She came to the United States as a young woman with her sister Catherine, answering a call for teachers. She helped found a Franciscan community in Joliet, Illinois, and later the Sisters of Saint Francis of Rochester, Minnesota. Her sisters ran schools for immigrant families.

Dr. Mayo turned the downtown dance hall into a temporary hospital after the tornado. Afterward, Moes proposed that Rochester needed a permanent hospital. By the account in Mayo Clinic's own history, Dr. Mayo at first told her the town was "too small to support a hospital," but he agreed. The sisters earned and saved the money themselves. They would build and run the hospital and train as nurses, and Dr. Mayo and his two sons would be its physicians.

Saint Marys Hospital opened in 1889. That partnership between immigrant Catholic sisters and a family of country doctors grew into what is now Mayo Clinic. Moes died in 1899, and the Rochester Franciscans still sponsor ministries in Minnesota.
keyFacts: 1828: Born October 28 in Remich, Luxembourg.
Helped found the Sisters of St. Francis in Joliet, Illinois, and the Sisters of Saint Francis of Rochester, Minnesota.
1883: Rochester tornado, August 21; her sisters nursed the injured.
1889: Saint Marys Hospital opened, built by the sisters, with the Mayos as its doctors.
1899: Died December 18.
people.connectToWork: Which well-known institutions in your work began as one immigrant or faith group's response to a need? What would change if you treated newer groups' institutions the same way?

people.name: Archbishop John Ireland
body: In 1852 a teenage boy from County Kilkenny, Ireland, arrived with his family in St. Paul, then a frontier town in Minnesota Territory. The Irelands had left during the years of the Great Famine, which killed about a million people in Ireland and drove millions more to emigrate.

St. Paul's first bishop, Joseph Crétin, chose young John Ireland for the priesthood and sent him to study in France. Ireland was ordained in St. Paul in 1861 and served as chaplain to the Fifth Minnesota Volunteer Infantry during the Civil War. He became coadjutor bishop in 1875, bishop of St. Paul in 1884, and St. Paul's first archbishop in 1888.

He believed that Irish families living in poverty in city slums would do better on farms. In 1876 he founded the Catholic Colonization Bureau, which worked with railroads to sell land to Catholic settlers in western and southwestern Minnesota. Towns such as Clontarf, Graceville and Minneota grew out of it. Not everything went well. In June 1880 a group of 50 very poor families, 309 people, arrived at Graceville from Connemara in western Ireland. Ireland gave each family 160 acres, clothing, supplies, seed and credit for food, but they came too late to plant and were unready for the winter of 1880–1881. In 1881 he moved them to St. Paul, where most settled in the neighborhood later called Connemara Patch. The bureau also never drew as many Irish settlers as he had hoped.

Ireland became a nationally known voice for "Americanizing" the Catholic Church. He argued that immigrants could keep their faith and also be fully American, which put him at odds with some German Catholic leaders who wanted services and schools in their own language. He promoted temperance, organizing a Father Mathew Total Abstinence Society chapter in 1869. He also raised money and gave land for the St. Thomas Aquinas Seminary, which led to the University of St. Thomas, and commissioned the Cathedral of Saint Paul, which held its first Mass in 1915. He died in St. Paul in 1918.
keyFacts: 1838: Born September 11 in Burnchurch, County Kilkenny, Ireland.
1852: Family arrived in St. Paul in May.
1861: Ordained a priest; chaplain to the Fifth Minnesota Volunteer Infantry.
1876: Founded the Catholic Colonization Bureau.
1888: Became the first Archbishop of St. Paul.
1918: Died September 25 in St. Paul.
people.connectToWork: When a program is designed to help people "get ahead", whose idea of a good life is built into it, and what happens to the people it does not fit, as with the Connemara families?

people.name: Ole Edvart Rølvaag
body: Rølvaag grew up on Dønna, an island off Norway's northern coast, in a family of fishermen, and as a young man he earned his living from the sea. He turned down command of a fishing boat, and in 1896 he emigrated to South Dakota, where he worked a year on his uncle's farm to save money for school.

He studied at Augustana, a small preparatory school in Canton, South Dakota, and then at St. Olaf College in Northfield, Minnesota, a school founded by Norwegian Lutherans. He graduated in 1905, spent a year studying in Oslo, and joined St. Olaf's faculty in 1906, where he taught Norwegian for about 25 years.

His best-known work, Giants in the Earth, first came out in Norwegian in two volumes, in 1924 and 1925. It appeared in English in 1927, translated with Lincoln Colcord. The novel follows Per Hansa and his wife Beret, Norwegian settlers in Dakota Territory. Per Hansa loves the challenge of the open prairie. Beret is crushed by its isolation and grieves the home she left. The book does not paint a rosy picture of pioneer life. It shows homesickness, depression and the losses that come with uprooting a family. Rølvaag continued the story in Peder Victorious and Their Fathers' God.

Rølvaag also argued that immigrants should keep their language and culture rather than drop them quickly. In 1925 he became the first secretary and archivist of the Norwegian-American Historical Association, which is still based at St. Olaf. He died in Northfield in 1931.
keyFacts: 1876: Born on the island of Dønna, Norway.
1896: Emigrated to the United States.
1905: Graduated from St. Olaf College; joined its faculty in 1906.
1925: First secretary and archivist of the Norwegian-American Historical Association.
1927: Giants in the Earth published in English.
1931: Died November 5 in Northfield, Minnesota.
people.connectToWork: What stories does your family or workplace tell about those who settled here? Whose loneliness, language loss or depression do those stories leave out, and does that shape what you expect of newcomers today?

people.name: Wanda Gág
body: In 1908 the artist Anton Gag died of tuberculosis in New Ulm, Minnesota. His eldest daughter, Wanda, was a teenager. Their mother was in poor health, and the family had seven children. Wanda helped support the family with her art, and she still finished high school in 1912.

The Gágs belonged to New Ulm's community of German-speaking immigrants from Bohemia, a region now in the Czech Republic. Wanda grew up surrounded by Old World folk tales, and she watched her father work as a painter.

She went on to the St. Paul Art School and the Minneapolis School of Art, and then won a scholarship to the Art Students League in New York, where she became a respected printmaker. Her 1928 picture book Millions of Cats was named a Newbery Honor book and is often called the oldest American picture book still in print. Her ABC Bunny won a second Newbery Honor. She also translated and illustrated Grimm's fairy tales, which took her back to the stories of her childhood, and her Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs and Nothing at All earned Caldecott Honors.
Gág died of lung cancer on June 27, 1946, in New York City. Her childhood home in New Ulm is now a museum listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
keyFacts: 1893: Born March 11 in New Ulm, Minnesota, to Bohemian immigrant parents.
1908: Her father died, leaving her the eldest of seven children.
1928: Published Millions of Cats, a Newbery Honor book.
1933: Published The ABC Bunny, also a Newbery Honor book.
1946: Died June 27 in New York City.
people.connectToWork: When a teenager is carrying adult duties at home, does your process notice? Would you read it differently depending on the family's name or background?

people.name: Fanny Fligelman Brin
people.field: Peace activism, women's civic leadership, Jewish community leadership
body: In 1921, as the world recovered from World War I, a Minneapolis woman became director of the Minneapolis Women's Committee for World Disarmament. Fanny Brin wanted women, who had only just won the vote, to use their new voice to prevent the next war.

She was born in Berlad (Bârlad), Romania, in 1884. Jews in Romania then faced harsh legal discrimination and were often denied citizenship. The Fligelmans left and joined Minneapolis's Romanian Jewish settlement while Fanny was still an infant. She grew up there and graduated Phi Beta Kappa from the University of Minnesota. In 1913 she married Arthur Brin, a glass merchant.

She did most of her work through the National Council of Jewish Women, a volunteer organization that had helped immigrants settle. From 1923 to 1929 she chaired its national peace and arbitration committee, and in 1924 she became president of the Minneapolis section. In 1932 she was elected national president, serving until 1938, and she moved the organization toward education about peace and international affairs. She backed the Kellogg-Briand Pact, a treaty to outlaw war, and Carrie Chapman Catt asked her to lead the Minnesota campaign for it. During the Nazi era the council also took part in the German Jewish Children's Aid program, which brought Jewish children to America from 1934 on.
She died in Minneapolis in 1961.
keyFacts: 1884: Born October 20 in Berlad, Romania; family settled in Minneapolis.
Graduated with honors from the University of Minnesota.
1921: Director of the Minneapolis Women's Committee for World Disarmament.
1932–1938: National president of the National Council of Jewish Women.
1961: Died September 4 in Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: When you hear "European American" or "white" at work, who gets folded in without being asked, and how might a Jewish colleague or client experience that?

people.name: Rudy Perpich
body: Rudy Perpich grew up in Carson Lake, a mining location that is now part of Hibbing on Minnesota's Iron Range. His father had come from Croatia to work in the iron mines, and his mother was the daughter of Croatian immigrants. Rudy did not speak English when he started school.

Perpich opened a dental office in Hibbing in 1954 and practiced there until 1974, according to the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library. He won a seat on the Hibbing school board in 1955, where he and his colleagues voted to give female teachers equal pay. He served in the state senate from 1963 to 1971 and was elected lieutenant governor in 1970.

In December 1976, when Governor Wendell Anderson resigned to take a U.S. Senate seat, Perpich became governor. He lost the 1978 election, then won again in 1982 and served from 1983 to 1991, the first Minnesota governor to serve non-consecutive terms. He lost to Arne Carlson in 1990. In 1991 he moved to Zagreb to work as a consultant to the newly independent Croatian government.

As governor he pushed education and economic development and backed what became the Perpich Center for Arts Education and its arts high school. He was known for big, unusual ideas, and critics often mocked him for them. MNopedia notes that he appointed more women to public office than any previous Minnesota governor, including Rosalie Wahl, the first woman on the Minnesota Supreme Court. He died of colon cancer at his Minnetonka home in 1995.
keyFacts: 1928: Born June 27 in Carson Lake, now Hibbing, to a Croatian immigrant miner.
1954: Opened a dental office in Hibbing, where he practiced until 1974.
1976: Became governor on December 29 after Wendell Anderson resigned; served until January 1979.
1983–1991: Second period as governor.
1995: Died September 21 in Minnetonka.
people.connectToWork: If a child starts school in your area without English today, what do people assume about the family? Would they assume the same about a miner's son from the Iron Range in the 1930s?

people.name: Charles A. Lindbergh
body: On May 20–21, 1927, a 25-year-old pilot flew alone from New York to Paris, about 33½ hours without stopping. Charles Lindbergh became one of the most famous people on earth almost overnight. He was born in Detroit and grew up in Little Falls, Minnesota, in a house that is now a state historic site.

His Swedish roots are more complicated than the legend. According to the Minnesota Historical Society, his grandfather, August Lindbergh, was a member of Sweden's parliament who was charged with illegal banking activities. Around 1859 he emigrated with his infant son and settled in Melrose, Minnesota. That son, renamed Charles August Lindbergh, became a lawyer in Little Falls and served ten years as a U.S. congressman from Minnesota.

After the flight, Lindbergh promoted commercial aviation and worked with the scientist Alexis Carrel on an early perfusion pump, a device for keeping organs alive outside the body. In 1932 his infant son was kidnapped and murdered. Before World War II he became the leading speaker for the America First Committee, which opposed U.S. involvement in the war. At a rally in Des Moines on September 11, 1941, he accused Britain, Jews and the Roosevelt administration of pushing the country toward war. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the speech as repeating antisemitic lies.
Later in life he became a conservation advocate. He died at his home on Maui, Hawaii, in August 1974.
keyFacts: 1902: Born February 4 in Detroit; raised in Little Falls, Minnesota.
About 1859: Swedish grandfather August Lindbergh emigrated to Melrose, Minnesota.
1927: First solo nonstop transatlantic flight, New York to Paris, May 20–21 (33 hours, 30 minutes).
1941: Des Moines "war agitators" speech for the America First Committee, September 11.
1974: Died August 26 on Maui, Hawaii.
people.connectToWork: Which local heroes does your workplace or town celebrate, and what would it take to tell the harm alongside the achievement with the people that harm was aimed at?

people.name: Fiorello La Guardia
body: From 1907 to 1910, newcomers at Ellis Island sometimes met a young interpreter who could talk with them in Italian, German, Yiddish or Croatian. Fiorello La Guardia was working there by day while studying law at night. He later wrote about those years in his autobiography, The Making of an Insurgent.

His own background crossed several European lines. His father, Achille, was an Italian musician from southern Italy. His mother, Irene Luzzato Coen, came from a Jewish family in Trieste, then part of Austria-Hungary. Fiorello was born in New York and grew up partly on Army posts in Arizona, where his father was a bandmaster. As a young man he worked at the American consulate in Budapest and then as U.S. consular agent in Fiume, now Rijeka, Croatia, where he handled emigrants leaving for America and insisted they be medically examined before they boarded.

La Guardia became a lawyer and went into politics. During World War I he flew in Italy and left the service as a major. He served in Congress, opposed racist immigration policies and co-sponsored the Norris–La Guardia Act of 1932, which limited the courts' power to block strikes, boycotts and picketing.

He was elected mayor of New York and served three terms, from 1934 to 1945. During the 1945 newspaper deliverers' strike, he read the Sunday comics, including Dick Tracy, over the city's radio station WNYC so children would not miss them. LaGuardia Airport is named for him. He died in the Bronx on September 20, 1947.
keyFacts: 1882: Born December 11 in New York City, to an Italian father and a Jewish mother from Trieste.
1903–1906: U.S. consular agent in Fiume, now Rijeka, Croatia.
1907–1910: Interpreter at Ellis Island (Italian, German, Yiddish, Croatian).
1932: Co-sponsored the Norris–La Guardia Act.
1934–1945: Mayor of New York City for three terms.
1947: Died September 20.
people.connectToWork: Who interprets at the front door of your service, and what do they see about your process that nobody asks them about?

people.name: Barbara Mikulski
body: In 1969, highway planners wanted to run an East-West Expressway through the old Polish and working-class neighborhoods of East Baltimore. A young social worker named Barbara Mikulski helped found a group of residents to stop it. That neighborhood fight started her political career.

Mikulski grew up in Highlandtown, East Baltimore. Her immigrant grandmother opened a bakery, and her parents ran a neighborhood grocery store. She earned a master's degree in social work from the University of Maryland in 1965, and her first job was with Catholic Charities, working with children in foster care and group homes.

She won a seat on the Baltimore City Council in 1971. She served in the U.S. House from 1977 to 1987 and in the Senate from 1987 to 2017. She was the first Democratic woman elected to the Senate without first being appointed or succeeding her husband. In March 2012 she became the longest-serving woman in the history of Congress, and later that year she became the first woman to chair the Senate Appropriations Committee. President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015. In September 2026 current and former lawmakers gathered on Capitol Hill to mark her 90th birthday.
keyFacts: 1936: Born July 20 in Baltimore, Maryland, to Polish American parents.
Social worker before entering politics; elected to the Baltimore City Council in 1971.
1977–1987: U.S. House of Representatives.
1987–2017: U.S. Senate; in March 2012 became the longest-serving woman in congressional history.
2012: First woman to chair the Senate Appropriations Committee.
2015: Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: Norman Borlaug
body: In July 1944 a young plant scientist trained at the University of Minnesota flew to Mexico City to lead a wheat research program. Norman Borlaug became the scientist most associated with the "Green Revolution."

Borlaug was born on March 25, 1914, in Saude, Iowa, a Norwegian American farming community, to parents descended from Norwegian immigrants. In 1933, at age 19, he arrived at the University of Minnesota. Over the next nine years he earned a bachelor's degree in forestry and a master's and a doctorate in plant pathology, studying under Professor Elvin C. Stakman.

In Mexico, Borlaug and his colleagues bred wheat varieties that resisted disease and gave higher yields. In 1965 he helped send semi-dwarf wheat seed to Pakistan and India, at a time when both countries feared famine. By the Academy of Achievement's account, Pakistan became self-sufficient in wheat by 1968, and India in all cereal crops by 1974.

In 1970 Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize for his contributions to the world food supply. In 1986 he created the World Food Prize. Congress voted him its Gold Medal in 2006, and President George W. Bush presented it in the Capitol Rotunda on July 17, 2007. He died in Dallas, Texas, on September 12, 2009, at age 95.
keyFacts: 1914: Born March 25 in Saude, Iowa, to a Norwegian American farm family.
1933: Entered the University of Minnesota; later earned a B.S. in forestry and an M.S. and Ph.D. in plant pathology.
1944: Went to Mexico to lead a wheat research program.
1965: Helped send semi-dwarf wheat seed to India and Pakistan.
1970: Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize; 1986: Created the World Food Prize.
2009: Died September 12 in Dallas, Texas.
people.connectToWork: What knowledge does someone with a farming background bring that your intake or hiring process never asks about? Do you see that knowledge differently depending on where the farm was?

people.name: Greta Garbo
body: In 1930 movie posters across America carried two words: "Garbo talks!" Audiences had loved Greta Garbo in silent films. Anna Christie was the first time they would hear her voice, accented by her Swedish childhood. The film earned her an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress.

She was born Greta Lovisa Gustafsson on September 18, 1905, in the Södermalm district of Stockholm. As a young woman she worked at Stockholm's PUB department store, running errands and modeling hats, and then as a fashion model at Nordiska Kompaniet. Her film career began in Sweden. MGM's Louis B. Mayer offered contracts to her and her mentor, director Mauritz Stiller; EBSCO reports that Mayer mainly wanted Stiller, who refused to come without her.

Her first American film was The Torrent (1926), and Flesh and the Devil made her an international star. She went on to star in Grand Hotel (1932), Queen Christina (1933) and Camille (1936), and a 1933 contract made her the highest-paid actress in Hollywood. Ninotchka (1939), a comedy, was advertised with the line "Garbo laughs." She received Best Actress nominations for Anna Christie, Camille and Ninotchka.

In 1941, after Two-Faced Woman, she stopped making films. She was not yet 40. She chose a private life in New York City and became a U.S. citizen on February 9, 1951. She received the Academy's honorary award for 1954, presented in 1955, and did not attend the ceremony. She died in New York City on April 15, 1990.
keyFacts: 1905: Born Greta Lovisa Gustafsson on September 18 in Stockholm, Sweden.
1926: First American film, The Torrent, for MGM.
1930: First sound film, Anna Christie, marketed as "Garbo talks!"
1941: Stopped making films after Two-Faced Woman.
1951: Became a U.S. citizen on February 9.
1990: Died April 15 in New York City.
people.connectToWork: Which accents does your workplace hear as charming and which as a barrier? What does that show you about your own ear?

people.name: Knute Rockne
body: On November 1, 1913, the small Catholic college of Notre Dame played Army at West Point. Quarterback Gus Dorais threw long forward passes to an end named Knute Rockne, and Notre Dame won 35–13. That game helped show the nation what the forward pass could do.

Rockne was born in 1888 in Voss, Norway. When he was five, his family emigrated and settled in Chicago's Logan Square neighborhood. At Notre Dame he was a second-team All-American in 1913 and a serious student. He earned a degree in pharmacy and chemistry in 1914 and worked as a lab assistant to the chemist Julius Nieuwland, and then turned to coaching.

As Notre Dame's head coach from 1918 to 1930, Rockne won 105 games, lost 12 and tied 5. EBSCO calls his .881 winning percentage the highest of any major college football coach. Notre Dame credits his teams with national championships in 1924, 1929 and 1930; EBSCO credits six.

On March 31, 1931, Rockne, then 43, was killed when his passenger plane came down in a cow pasture just south of Bazaar, in Chase County, Kansas. He had been hired as a consultant on the film The Spirit of Notre Dame.
keyFacts: 1888: Born in Voss, Norway; emigrated with his family at age five to Chicago.
1913: Caught forward passes from Gus Dorais in Notre Dame's 35–13 win over Army, November 1.
1914: Graduated from Notre Dame with a degree in pharmacy and chemistry.
1918–1930: Notre Dame head coach, with a record of 105–12–5.
1931: Killed at age 43 in a plane crash near Bazaar, Kansas, March 31.

people.name: Maria von Trapp
body: In December 1938 a family choir from Austria walked onto the stage of New York's Town Hall. They had fled their homeland that September, after Nazi Germany annexed Austria. Leading them was Maria von Trapp, whose life story would later be told in The Sound of Music.

Maria Augusta Kutschera was born on January 26, 1905, on a train headed to Vienna. She married into the von Trapp family, and the family made music together. When they left Austria, they traveled through Italy and England before reaching the United States.

In America the choir took the name the Trapp Family Singers, on the advice of an agent. They first lived in Merion, Pennsylvania, and in 1942 bought a farm in Stowe, Vermont, which became the Trapp Family Lodge. The family's resort dates their final U.S. concert to 1956, and EBSCO dates the choir's end to 1957.

After World War II, the family founded the Trapp Family Austrian Relief fund, which sent food and clothing to people in Austria. In 1948 Pope Pius XII honored Maria with the Bene Merenti Medal for this work. In 1949 she published her memoir, The Trapp Family Singers, which inspired a 1956 German film, the 1959 Broadway musical The Sound of Music and the 1965 film. Her son Johannes took over the lodge from her in 1969. She died on March 28, 1987, and is buried at the lodge.
keyFacts: 1905: Born Maria Augusta Kutschera on January 26, on a train bound for Vienna.
1938: Fled Austria in September; New York Town Hall concert in December.
1942: Bought a farm in Stowe, Vermont.
After World War II: Founded the Trapp Family Austrian Relief fund.
1949: Published The Trapp Family Singers.
1959 and 1965: Broadway musical and film The Sound of Music, based on her memoir.
1987: Died March 28; buried at the family lodge in Stowe.

people.name: Walter Mondale
body: In 1993 a former vice president from small-town Minnesota arrived in Tokyo as the U.S. Ambassador to Japan. Walter Mondale served there until 1996. It was the international chapter of a long public career.

Mondale was born on January 5, 1928, in Ceylon, in Martin County, and grew up in nearby Elmore. MNopedia describes him as a Norwegian Minnesotan. His father was a Methodist minister and his mother a music teacher. The foreclosure of his father's farms in the 1920s influenced him as a young man.

He studied at Macalester College, graduated from the University of Minnesota in 1951, served in the Army at Fort Knox during the Korean War, and earned his University of Minnesota law degree in 1956. In 1960, at age 32, he was appointed Minnesota Attorney General. In 1964 he was appointed to the U.S. Senate, and he served until 1976. From 1977 to 1981 he was Vice President under Jimmy Carter. In 1984 he was the Democratic nominee for president and chose Geraldine Ferraro as his running mate, the first woman on a major-party presidential ticket.
He served as ambassador to Japan under President Bill Clinton, and in 1998 as a special envoy to Indonesia. He died at his home in Minneapolis on April 19, 2021, at age 93.
keyFacts: 1928: Born January 5 in Ceylon, Minnesota; raised in Elmore.
1956: Law degree from the University of Minnesota.
1960: Appointed Minnesota Attorney General at age 32.
1964–1976: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; 1977–1981: Vice President.
1993–1996: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; 1998: special envoy to Indonesia.
2021: Died April 19 in Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: What did a family's money trouble, such as a farm foreclosure, teach you to expect from public institutions? How would you ask someone else what theirs taught them?

people.name: Muriel Humphrey Brown
body: Muriel Fay Buck was born on February 20, 1912, in Huron, South Dakota, and married Hubert H. Humphrey. Her granddaughter Vicky Solomonson, profiled on this page, was born with Down syndrome in 1960. Vicky enrolled in the Fraser Home Study School in Minneapolis, and Fraser's history records that Muriel soon got involved with the school.

She became an advocate for people with Down syndrome and for moving people out of institutions and into group homes in the community. Fraser established the Muriel Humphrey Residences in 1977, three group homes serving 12 residents each.

After Hubert Humphrey's death in January 1978, Governor Rudy Perpich asked her to complete his term in the U.S. Senate, and she did. She later married Max Brown. She died in September 1998 in Minneapolis at age 86. At her memorial, Fraser's executive director said, "Because of Muriel, we have come a long way."
keyFacts: 1912: Born February 20 in Huron, South Dakota.
Advocated moving people from institutions to group homes.
1977: Fraser established the Muriel Humphrey Residences.
1978: Appointed to complete Hubert Humphrey's U.S. Senate term.
1998: Died in September in Minneapolis, age 86.

people.name: Vicky Solomonson
body: Victoria "Vicky" Solomonson was born on election night 1960 and had Down syndrome. Doctors suggested institutionalization. Her parents, Bruce and Nancy Solomonson, refused and raised her at home with help from her grandparents, Hubert and Muriel Humphrey. MPR News described her as "perhaps best known as a symbol of the disabilities rights movement."

Her own life was more than a symbol. By the Star Tribune's account, she lived in Fraser residences for people with disabilities, worked with Opportunity Partners and took pride in earning a paycheck. She enjoyed swimming, horseback riding and bowling, and she lived with friends in Hopkins. She died in May 2010 at 49, of Alzheimer's disease. We found no record of her own words, so what is written about her comes from others.
keyFacts: 1960: Born on election night.
Raised at home against medical advice.
Lived in Fraser residences and worked with Opportunity Partners.
2010: Died in May, age 49.

institutions.name: American Swedish Institute
body: On Park Avenue in south Minneapolis stands a turreted mansion that looks like a castle. It was built between 1903 and 1908 for Swan Turnblad, a Swedish immigrant who published Svenska Amerikanska Posten, a Swedish-language newspaper that was likely the main source of his wealth.

On December 9, 1929, Turnblad donated the house, the newspaper, and his books and artifacts to found what was then called the American Institute for Swedish Arts, Literature and Science. It became the American Swedish Institute.

In 2012 ASI opened the Nelson Cultural Center beside the mansion. Today it presents exhibitions from Sweden and the Nordic region, youth and family programs, performing arts, language and Nordic handcraft classes, and the FIKA café. It describes itself as an arts and cultural organization that "engages locally and connects globally."
keyFacts: 1903–1908: Turnblad mansion built at 2600 Park Avenue.
1929: Turnblad donated the house and newspaper to found the institute.
2012: Nelson Cultural Center opened.
Turnblad Mansion: three stories, 33 rooms.
institutions.connectToWork: Some immigrant newspapers and cultural centers end up as landmarks. Which newer community media and gathering places in your area does your team treat as just as serious a partner?

institutions.name: Sons of Norway
aliases: Independent Order of the Sons of Norway
institutions.location: 1455 West Lake Street, Minneapolis; lodges in the U.S., Canada and Norway
body: On January 16, 1895, eighteen Norwegian immigrants in Minneapolis formed the Independent Order of the Sons of Norway. Their reason was practical. By MNopedia's account, many immigrants could not get life insurance on their own, so the members agreed to insure one another. The founders had first conceived the idea in 1893, during a severe economic downturn.

Its building at 1455 West Lake Street opened in 1962. In August 2017 it agreed to sell the 60,000-square-foot building and parking lot to developers, with plans to keep its business operations on the redeveloped site, and it still lists that address as its headquarters.

In May 2026 Sons of Norway announced an agreement to join BetterLife, another fraternal organization, subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions, with the deal expected to close later in the summer and full integration by year-end. It said it would continue as Sons of Norway within BetterLife.
keyFacts: 1895: Founded in Minneapolis by 18 members as a mutual-insurance society, January 16.
1962: Sons of Norway Building opened at 1455 West Lake Street.
2017: Lake Street property sold to developers.
2026: Announced an agreement to join BetterLife, subject to regulatory approval.
institutions.connectToWork: If immigrants pooling money to insure one another is respectable history, how does your program read similar savings and mutual-aid networks today, including on a benefits form?

institutions.name: Germanic-American Institute
body: In 1957 Minnesota celebrated its centennial as a state, and German clubs in the Twin Cities joined to form the Volksfest Association to represent German Minnesotans. In 1965 the association bought a 1906 house on Summit Avenue for $57,500 from the Sisters of St. Benedict, who had owned it since 1948, and named it the Volksfest Kulturhaus ("culture house").

In 1994, facing generational change, members turned the social club into a nonprofit, the Germanic-American Institute. In 2005 it founded the Twin Cities German Immersion School. Today it offers adult German classes and youth programs for ages 3 to 18, including the Kinderstube immersion preschool, and it is a Goethe-Institut partner society. It also runs St. Paul Oktoberfest, held September 11–12 in 2026.
The institute says that as a German American organization it carries a "historical responsibility" to be a warning voice when fear, hatred and xenophobia take root.
keyFacts: 1957: Volksfest Association formed for Minnesota's centennial.
1965: Bought the 1906 house at 301 Summit Avenue for $57,500.
1994: Became the nonprofit Germanic-American Institute.
2005: Founded the Twin Cities German Immersion School.

institutions.name: Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota
body: In 1865, Pastor Eric Norelius of Red Wing took in four children whose parents had died in St. Paul. They were first cared for at the Vasa Church, a Swedish Lutheran congregation. That work became the Vasa Children's Home, which its centennial history calls the oldest home in Minnesota and the Augustana Lutheran Church. In 1876 Norelius offered it to the church's Minnesota Conference, and in 1926 it moved to a new site.

In September 1954 the home began caring for children with intellectual disabilities. The work grew into Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota, formed in 1963 when the Board of Christian Service and the Lutheran Welfare Society merged. In 2003 LSS completed a renovation of Camp Knutson, a camp for children with identified needs, and in 2021 Lifetrack began delivering services as part of LSS, adding Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services, an Early Learning Center and employment services.
keyFacts: 1865: Vasa Children's Home begun by Pastor Eric Norelius.
1876: Given to the Minnesota Conference of the Augustana Synod; moved to a new site in 1926.
1954: Began caring for children with intellectual disabilities.
1963: LSS formed by merger.
2021: Lifetrack services joined LSS.

institutions.name: The Arc Minnesota
body: In December 1946, Evelyn Carlson and Reuben Lindh formed the Minneapolis Association of Retarded Children, later known as The Arc, according to the Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities. It began with concerned parents looking for something better than the conditions at state institutions.

On September 28, 1950, parents from across the country met in Minneapolis for the first national convention that formed The Arc. Governor Luther Youngdahl spoke there on the rights of people with developmental disabilities, including the right to live with a family and to go to school. The state office opened in May 1957, with Jerry Walsh as its first executive director.

The organization's old names used language it now rejects, and The Arc's national history says so directly. Today The Arc Minnesota offers advocates who give information and support to people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, their families and trusted supporters.
keyFacts: 1946: Minneapolis parents' group formed in December.
1950: First national convention held in Minneapolis, September 28.
1957: State office opened in May under Jerry Walsh.
institutions.connectToWork: This parent movement began with families asking the state for something better. How does your team respond when parents today organize and push back?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, European American means Minnesotans of many heritages, including Scandinavian, German, Irish, Polish, Finnish and others, across several generations, urban and rural places, and many faiths or none. We did not find a study of how European American Minnesotans as a group understand disability. What follows draws on Minnesota's own disability history, which families and church institutions of European heritage helped shape, and on one small study of U.S. and Danish families, labeled as such. Treat every point as something to ask about.
questions: Who in your family helps with care, and who would you like involved in decisions?
Have you or older relatives had experiences with institutions or state services that shape how you feel about help now?
Is a faith community, congregation or church-affiliated agency part of your support? Would you like it to be?
Some families prefer to handle things privately. What would make it easier to accept outside help?
What words do you use for your disability, and what words would you like us to use?
How far are you from the services you need, and what about transportation or online options?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you worry it might close off?

context.heading: What older relatives may remember
body: The Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities describes a mid-20th-century pattern in which babies with developmental disabilities were often sent to state institutions such as Faribault and Cambridge, which were badly overcrowded. By 1954 the waiting list had reached 884 children. The same history records that some parents turned their babies over in their strollers so others would not see a child's disability.

People who lived through this are now grandparents and great-grandparents. Ask what they remember, and do not assume. Staff should not read a family's caution about services as a lack of interest in help.

sources.label: Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, 1940s to 50s: Lighting the Fire
Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, Parallels in Time, 1940s

context.heading: Parents who pushed back
body: The same history records that families organized. In 1950 the first national convention of what is now The Arc met in Minneapolis, and Governor Youngdahl's list of rights there included the right to live with a family.

One family's story shows how this could look. After Vicky Solomonson was born with Down syndrome in 1960, her parents refused doctors' advice to institutionalize her and raised her at home with help from her grandparents, Hubert and Muriel Humphrey. This is one well-known family with public standing. It is not a pattern, and it does not tell you how any family decides.

sources.label: Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, 1940s to 50s: Lighting the Fire

context.heading: What one study asked about stigma
body: Fujii and Shiraishi (2000) surveyed families of people with developmental disabilities in Japan, Denmark and the United States. U.S. families reported much stronger stigma than Danish families, on measures such as feeling inadequate as a family, perceived prejudice and anxiety about the future. The authors connected lower stigma to better social support systems. The U.S. and Danish samples were small, 46 and 56 families, and the study is not about Minnesotans or about European Americans specifically. It says nothing about any one family.

sources.label: Fujii and Shiraishi, Japanese Journal of Social Services 2 (2000): 101–109

context.heading: When church agencies are the formal system
body: For some Minnesotans of European heritage, a church-affiliated agency is not an alternative to the formal system. It is the formal system. Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota, profiled on this page, grew from a Swedish Lutheran congregation's care for orphans and now provides disability services statewide. We did not research Catholic Charities in depth here.

Some people may trust a church-affiliated provider more readily, and others may prefer a secular one. Ask, and never assume a person's faith from a surname or heritage. We found no research on religious explanations of disability in this population, so none is described here. With the person's consent, a pastor, parish nurse or congregation can be part of planning.

sources.label: VCU Social Welfare History Project, History of the Vasa Children's Home (1865–1955)
Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota, Our History

context.heading: Words, language and distance
body: Older official terms that are now considered offensive were standard during many older relatives' lives, and they appeared in the names of disability organizations. The Arc of the United States says its former legal names included outdated language it rejects today. An older relative may still use those words without intending harm. Use current terms, and follow the disabled person's own preference.

Do not assume English is the only language at home. Offer plain-language materials and interpreters when needed. Some people live far from services, and in a small town privacy may be a real concern. See this collection's rural page for more about place.

sources.label: The Arc of the United States, Our History

organizations.intro: Organizing around European heritage in Minnesota today centers on cultural centers, fraternal societies, congregations and festivals. Events with 2026 dates include New Ulm Oktoberfest (Oct. 2-3 and 9-10), FinnFest USA in Minneapolis (Sept. 17-20, with a larger Minneapolis festival planned for September 2027), Mindekirken's Syttende Mai (May 17), St. Urho's Day in Finland, Minnesota (March 13-15) and St. Paul's 60th St. Patrick's Day parade. Spring Grove's Syttende Mai will be replaced by a Homecoming in June 2027. Earlier generations also built a large foreign-language press and their own mutual-aid societies: Minneapolis Tidende, a Norwegian-language paper published from 1895 to 1935, averaged a circulation of 32,000 in 1914, and the Polish White Eagle Association was a Minnesota fraternal society with a dozen local groups. We found no current activity for that association. These groups are not human-services providers, and we found no disability organization specific to this page. The list is a set of starting points for learning, it is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. Many of these groups reach members through their own newsletters, event calendars and social media, so check each one.

entries.name: Norway House
entries.purpose: Established in 2004. A nonprofit that says it connects the United States and contemporary Norway through arts, business and culture, with exhibits, events and a café. It also houses The Norwegian American newspaper.

entries.name: Danish American Center
entries.purpose: Created in 2005 by the merger of the Danish American Fellowship and the Danebo senior housing, and reported in 2024 to have about 800 members. Offers events, meals and social activities around Danish culture.

entries.name: Salolampi Foundation
entries.purpose: Formed in 1979. Supports the Salolampi Finnish Language Village, a program of Concordia Language Villages, with scholarships, fundraising and volunteer work weekends.

entries.name: Finlandia Foundation Northland
entries.purpose: A Minnesota chapter of Finlandia Foundation National, founded in 2010. The national chapter list also names the Finnish American Association of the Twin Cities and a Hibbing chapter.
entries.linkLabel: Chapter list from Finlandia Foundation National

entries.name: SISU Heritage
entries.purpose: Oversees the Hanka and Pyhala homesteads, the Nelimark museum and the Seitaniemi housebarn, and holds concerts and community events.

entries.name: Sokol Minnesota
entries.location: St. Paul, C.S.P.S. Hall, 383 West Michigan Street
entries.purpose: A Czech and Slovak social, cultural, educational and gymnastic organization whose local unit dates to 1882. It says it welcomes all, regardless of nationality and cultural background.

entries.name: St. Mary's Greek Orthodox Church
entries.purpose: Greek Orthodox parish that hosts the Taste of Greece festival; the festival's 2026 dates (listed as September 11–13) are unconfirmed.
entries.linkLabel: Minneapolis Greek Festival, hosted by the parish

entries.name: Celtic Junction Arts Center
entries.purpose: A building in the Hamline-Midway neighborhood for Irish and Irish American arts. The Center for Irish Music is based there.
entries.linkLabel: Center for Irish Music, based in the Celtic Junction building

entries.name: Irish Fair of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A nonprofit whose flagship event is the Twin Cities Irish Fest on Harriet Island. Visit Saint Paul gives the 2026 dates as August 7–9.

entries.name: Center for Irish Music
entries.location: St. Paul, 836 Prior Avenue North, Suite 400
entries.purpose: A nonprofit school founded in 2004 that teaches traditional Irish music to children and adults, with classes, private lessons, ensembles and summer camps.

entries.name: Polish American Cultural Institute of Minnesota
aliases: Polish American Cultural Institute of Minnesota (PACIM)
entries.location: St. Paul, 75 Fifth Street West, Suite 431
entries.purpose: Describes itself as a place to meet and learn about Polish American heritage, for multigenerational families and newcomers to Minnesota. Holds events through the year, including a reading group and a fall soup festival.

entries.name: Italian Cultural Center of Minneapolis/St. Paul
entries.purpose: A nonprofit founded in 2006 that offers Italian language classes and cultural events in the Twin Cities.

entries.name: Mindekirken
entries.purpose: A Lutheran congregation with Sunday services in English and Norwegian and a bilingual service on the last Sunday of each month. Programs include Norwegian language classes, a lutefisk dinner and a Santa Lucia pageant.

entries.name: The Norwegian American
entries.location: Minneapolis, at Norway House; national readership
entries.purpose: Says it has been publishing since 1889. Twelve issues a year in English, with two to three pages in Norwegian, covering news from Norway, heritage, business, food and the arts.

entries.name: Viking magazine
aliases: Sons of Norway Viking magazine and lodge newsletters
entries.purpose: The member magazine of Sons of Norway, a member benefit listed on its site. Local lodges also publish their own newsletters.

entries.name: American-Scandinavian Foundation
entries.purpose: Incorporated in 1911. Supports exchange between the U.S. and the Nordic countries through fellowships, grants, internships, publishing and cultural events.

entries.name: German-American Heritage Foundation of the USA
entries.purpose: Says it has represented German Americans since 1977. Runs the German-American Heritage Museum of the USA.

entries.name: Ancient Order of Hibernians
entries.purpose: Founded in 1836 in the Pennsylvania coal region and New York City. Promotes Irish culture and supports charitable work. We did not confirm a Minnesota division.

entries.name: Polish American Congress
entries.purpose: Created at the Congress of Polonia in Buffalo, New York, in 1944. An umbrella body for Americans of Polish descent with state divisions. We did not confirm a Minnesota division.

entries.name: Order Sons and Daughters of Italy in America
entries.purpose: Created in 1905 as a mutual aid society for Italian immigrants. Runs lodges, a foundation and Italian America magazine. Thomas A. Lupo was installed as national president in August 2025.

entries.name: Nordstjernan
entries.purpose: Published since 1872, covering Swedish and Swedish American culture, food, traditions, emigration history and Nordic news.

entries.name: IrishCentral
entries.location: New York, with an office in Dublin
entries.purpose: Launched in 2009 by Niall O'Dowd. News, history, travel, opinion and culture for Irish Americans and the wider diaspora.

entries.name: L'Italo-Americano
entries.purpose: Established in 1908 and calls itself the oldest Italian American newspaper in the U.S. Reports in Italian and English on culture, heritage, arts and history.

entries.name: The Polish Weekly
entries.purpose: Polish and Polish American news, culture, history and community life, in English and Polish.

entries.name: Irish Echo
entries.purpose: Established in 1928. Irish American news, immigration and culture, with a circulation in all 50 states by Echo Media's account.
